newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian oil exports seen stable in near term - trade.
newsitem.headline: Russian oil exports seen stable in near term - trade.

text.p: Russian oil exports to Mediterranean and European markets will be stable in the near term and are not hostage to Kremlin politics, oil sources said on Tuesday.
"Russian export volumes never react to what's going on politically in Russia -- they just need the money too much," said a Western executive at a U.S. major in Moscow.
"Until domestic demand picks up, you'll see the same export level, which is basically at capacity."
Concern over President Boris Yeltsin's health helped lift oil prices last week and left traders wondering where Russian export volumes could head as Yeltsin prepares for heart surgery.
But Russia-based traders were not worried.
"The volumes are going to stay the same -- they need the money, they need the outlets, they need the destinations," a Moscow-based Western trader said.

Russia is the world's third largest oil producer after Saudi Arabia and the U.S. Last year it sold around one-third of its 1995 output of 305 million tonnes (6.2 million barrels per day) outside the Commonwealth of Independent States.
Non-CIS exports in 1995 were 96.8 million tonnes, or 1.936 million bpd, State Customs Committee figures show.
Oil output has declined, but Russian exports, mostly of sour Urals blend, have edged up as the economy struggles and deliveries to former Soviet republics slip.
The 1997 draft budget says exports could drop two to three percent next year, but traders said this was unlikely.
"Supply (to the West) is not going to change -- all you may see is some changes in who is exporting," said the Western executive.
Some analysts said Russia could in theory boost crude exports even though pipelines are working at capacity, but added that nothing was likely in the near term.

"There is more export capacity available -- they could easily find an extra 10-15 million tonnes a year (200,000- 300,000 bpd) capacity with what they have," said energy specialist Matthew Sagers of PlanEcon in Washington.

Options include rail shipments, exports through the Polish port of Gdansk, ironing out bottlenecks that keep material backed up in storage tanks and using more large tankers at Russia's Black Sea export outlet of Novorossiisk.
But Sagers said higher exports were unlikely soon, since Russia was unable to improve use of its capacities. "They'll keep it at what it is now," he said.

A Western source said one small Russian producer with good quality crude would try to export some of its 100,000 tonnes a year (2,000 bpd) output by rail to Finland, but this was not a new trend. "Companies may start railing some stuff out, but it will be minimal," he said.
Russian export volumes fluctuate sharply on seasonal and maintenance factors at Novorossiisk, which handles about 30 percent of all Russian oil exports and often closes for repairs or storms.
The closures mean Novorossiisk volumes can fall to as low as 500,000 bpd in winter from summer peaks of around 800,000 bpd.
"The repairs to pipelines feeding Novorossiisk are the biggest factor influencing exports," said Vladimir Afanasyev of traders Alfa-Eko. "There really aren't any other factors."
Russia's crude exports outside the Commonwealth of Independent States slipped seven percent in August from July to 8.99 million tonnes, mostly due to port repairs.
